en: The Sūtra on the Origins of the Two Brahmins, Śvetavastra and Suvarṇadhvaja, Spoken by the Buddha.
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Dharma Master, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Shi Hu and others, by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was staying in the Abandoned Garden of the Deer Park at Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two brahmins, Śuklodana and Kātyāyana, who lived near the Buddha; they desired to seek ordination and take on the appearance of bhikṣus.
At that time, during the latter part of the day, the World-Honored One emerged from his chamber, proceeded to the Mṛgāramātṛ Hall, and began to walk back and forth in meditation.
Then, the white-robed brahmin, having seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, proceed to the Mṛgāramātṛ Hall and walk back and forth in meditation, spoke to the brahmin Suvarṇadhvaja, saying:
"Suvarṇadhvaja!"
The worldly amusements and all dharmas of pleasure are entirely mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Although I have performed these actions, they ultimately lack any reality; whether in body or mind, weariness soon arises.
Because his body and mind experience weariness and fatigue, he immediately gives rise to loss of mindfulness.
This cause of lost mindfulness is itself impermanent, not firm, not ultimate, and a phenomenon subject to disintegration.
"You should not now practice such methods for amusement and pleasure, namely, the ritual of fire-worship.
The brahmin Suvarṇadhvaja said,
"How do you know this?"
The layperson replied,
“I have heard this from the Venerable Gautama.
That Gautama possesses great eloquence and well understands this meaning.”
Regarding what he has said, as for the practice of fire-worship—namely, that which has been handed down from the ancient seers—he knows all such teachings on the ritual of fire-worship.
There was a certain class of sages who, having conceived erroneous views toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, engaged in the practice of fire-worship.

Their error consisted in mutual hatred and envy, seeking out one another's faults; because they thus gave rise to the causes of mutual transgression, the lifespans of sentient beings began to diminish and disappear.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, having exhausted their lifespan in another realm, come to be born here.

If they are able to purify themselves, renounce the household life for the homeless life, cultivate and increase their practice, and correspond with reality through right and wholesome attention, then—according to their form and mind—they enter *samādhi*. Following that concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), they are then able to recollect the events of their past lives.

These sentient beings do not delight in mutual hatred, jealousy, or seeking out each other's faults; because they do not give rise to those causes of transgression, this is what is permanent, this is what is firm, this is what is ultimate, and this is the nature that is indestructible.

Furthermore, if sentient beings watch for one another's shortcomings, because they mutually give rise to the causes of transgression, this is impermanent, this is not firm, this is not ultimate, and this is a phenomenon subject to disintegration.
Therefore, O brahmins, you should not practice in this manner; do not give rise to erroneous views by instituting the rite of fire-worship.
Kancana, do you understand?
"In the afternoon, this Blessed One will emerge from his chamber and go to the Mṛgāramātṛ Hall, where he will again practice walking meditation.
You should now be able to accompany me to the presence of the Blessed One, prostrate at his feet, and follow him as he practices walking meditation."
"That Buddha, the World-Honored One, will surely preach the Dharma for us according to our needs.
Then, the Brahmin Suvarṇadhvaja said, "Excellent! I shall go."
At that time, the two brahmins, Śuklodana and Suvarṇadhvaja, having consulted with one another, went together to where the Buddha was.
Upon arrival, they simultaneously prostrated themselves at his feet and followed the Buddha as he walked in meditation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the two brahmins, Baiyi and Jintang, saying:

"You should know that all these brahmins claim to have mastered the Three Vedas; they are renowned as a superior lineage, pure of birth, born from a noble family of the Fire-God (Agni), with pure fathers and pure mothers, well-born of good stock, and even for seven generations their parents have been exalted and their lineage preeminent, free from fault and blame—all this is because their lineage is pure."

Furthermore, it is said that he thoroughly mastered and clearly understood five types of expository discourse: first, the ultimate three knowledges (*vidyā*) regarding the principles of the *mātṛkā*; second, the fixed names of all things; third, *ghaṭapana*; fourth, phonemes, syllables, and phrases; and fifth, elegant speech for playful discourse.
"Regarding these treatises on the prognostications and the various Vedic scriptures, the original teachers, the Brahmins, are thoroughly proficient in them. Layman!
Among the three Vedas, could there not be instances of disparagement, humiliation, and slander directed at the Brahmins?"
The two brahmins, Baiyi and Jintang, together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among the three Vedas, how may the various brahmins avoid being treated with contempt, insulted, or subjected to slander?”
Furthermore, within the scriptures of the three Vedas, the Brahmins speak thus:
"All Brahmins who are so purified are true Brahmins; they are sons of Brahmā, born from the pure mouth of Brahmā, of the lineage of Brahmā, emanated by Brahmā, and bestowed by Brahmā."
"Therefore, O brahmins, those who are thus pure are true brahmins.
"World-Honored One!
Yet we, the white-robed ones and the Golden Banner, are likewise entangled by our kinsmen; we have not attained liberation, but have diminished wholesome dharmas and increased unwholesome dharmas."
“World-Honored One!
This, too, constitutes for me, a brahmin, matters of being slighted, humiliated, and reviled within the Three Vedas.
The Buddha addressed the two brahmins, Baiyi and Jindang, saying:
“You should know this: the reason those brahmins incur contempt and slander within the Three Vedas is because the brahmins themselves speak thus:

‘All brahmins are pure in this way; they are true brahmins, sons of Brahmā, born from the pure mouth of Brahmā, of the lineage of Brahmā, emanated by Brahmā, and bestowed by Brahmā. Therefore, all brahmins are pure in this way; they are true brahmins.’”
"O lay follower!
Although those brahmins speak thus, they instead bring about their own ruin; they weaken themselves and further suffer loss.

That which those brahmins destroy is due to their giving rise to various attachments based on what is unreal, and consequently developing revulsion toward the True Dharma; from this, they immediately give rise to mutual contention and debate."
Why is this? Layman!

There are some brahmins who claim that at the time of birth there is a distinction of time, and while in the womb there is also a distinction; they cling to their own view, asserting that because the time of birth is distinct, it constitutes purity.
Furthermore, all these brahmins are likewise born from such purity; therefore, they speak thus:

"All brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his pure mouth; they are of Brahmā’s lineage, emanated by Brahmā, and bestowed by Brahmā. For this reason, all brahmins are thus pure; they are true brahmins."
"Householder!
You should know that there are four types, which constitute the four castes. What are these four?"
These are the kṣatriya caste, the brāhmaṇa caste, the vaiśya caste, and the śūdra caste.
Householder!

Among these four castes, those who perform black deeds experience the retribution of black deeds; such actions are not superior, are censured and loathed by the wise, and lead to rebirth in the evil destinies after death.

Furthermore, among the four castes, there are those who perform white karma and experience the retribution of white karma; this is a superior deed praised by the wise, and upon death, such a person is reborn in the celestial realms.
"Householder!
What is black karma?
It refers to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view; these are black karmas."
What is white karma?

It refers to not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not engaging in frivolous speech, not engaging in divisive speech, not engaging in harsh speech, not coveting, not being angry, and holding right view; these constitute white karma.
"Furthermore, lay follower!
Do not give rise to this thought: 'These dark karmas, such as killing and so forth, result in dark karmic retributions; they are not superior deeds and are censured and loathed by the wise. "
Among those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, all such things exist;
yet among the Brāhmaṇas alone, such things do not exist.
The two brahmins, Śuklodana and Suvarṇadhvaja, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why do you speak these words?”
This is not the case.
If one who performs black karma experiences the retribution of black karma, this applies to all kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras;
why then would the brāhmaṇas alone be exempt from it?
The Buddha said:
"Householder!

You must not again give rise to this thought, claiming that the various dark karmas exist among the other three castes but do not exist among the brahmins, and that such a statement constitutes a discourse consistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas."
Because the brahmin is a son of Brahmā, born from the pure mouth, of the lineage of Brahmā, emanated by Brahmā, and bestowed by Brahmā; being pure by birth, he is therefore a true brahmin.
“O White-robed One!
You must not again give rise to this thought: that if all four castes possess black karma, this statement would be inconsistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas.”
Furthermore, householder!
Do not give rise to this thought: that these white karmas, such as abstaining from taking life, produce white karmic results, and that this is a superior practice praised by the wise.
Among those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, none possess such a thing;
yet among the Brāhmaṇas alone does this exist.
The two brahmins, Śuklodana and Suvarṇadhvaja, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why do you speak these words?”
This is not so. If one performs white karma, one will experience the retribution of white karma.
This applies to all kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras alike.
"And why, layman, would only the Brahmins possess such [wrong views]?
The Buddha said: "Layman!"

Furthermore, do not give rise to this thought: that the white karmas exist among the Brahmins but not among the other three castes, and that this statement constitutes a teaching consistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas.
Because the brāhmaṇa is a son of Brahmā, born from the pure mouth, of the lineage of Brahmā, emanated by Brahmā, bestowed by Brahmā, and pure by birth, he is therefore a true brāhmaṇa.
“White-robed one!
You must not give rise to this thought again: that if all four castes possess white karma, this statement would be inconsistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas.”
Furthermore, lay follower!

Do not give rise to this thought: that among the various castes—Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—who commit black deeds such as killing, their bodies will break up at the end of life and they will fall into hell;
whereas for the Brāhmaṇas alone, this does not happen.
The two brahmins, Baiyi and Jintang, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why do you speak these words?”
This is not so. Among the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, those who commit black deeds all fall into hell when their bodies perish and their lives end;
yet why should the brāhmaṇas alone be exempt from evil?
The Buddha said, “Householder!

You must not again give rise to this thought: ‘Only the other three castes, but not the Brahmins, fall into hell for having committed black karma’—to say such a thing is merely a statement consistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas.”
Because the brāhmaṇa is a son of Brahmā, born from the pure mouth, of the lineage of Brahmā, emanated by Brahmā, bestowed by Brahmā, and pure by birth, he is a true brāhmaṇa.
"O White-robed One!

You must not again give rise to this thought: that because there is black karma among the four castes, they all fall into hell; such a statement is inconsistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas."
"Furthermore, lay follower!
Do not give rise to this thought: 'Because I have performed various white karmas such as abstaining from killing, when my body breaks up at the end of life, I will be reborn in the heavenly realms.'"
“Those among the kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras all lack such things;
yet the brāhmaṇas alone possess them.
The two brāhmaṇas, Śuklodana and Kāñcanabindu, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why do you speak thus?
This matter is not so.”
All kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras who perform wholesome deeds are reborn in the heavenly realms after the dissolution of the body and the end of life;
so why should this be otherwise for the brāhmaṇas alone?
The Buddha said:
"Householder!

You must not again give rise to this thought, namely, that while the Brahmins possess the creation of white karma leading to rebirth in the heavenly realms, the other three castes do not; such a claim is merely a statement consistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas."
Because the brahmin is a son of Brahmā, born from the pure mouth, of the lineage of Brahmā, emanated by Brahmā, and bestowed by Brahmā; since his original birth is pure, he is truly a brahmin.
“O White-clad One!

You must not again give rise to this thought: that because there is white karma among the four castes, they are all reborn in the heavenly realms; such a statement is inconsistent with the scriptures of the Three Vedas.”
Furthermore, lay follower!

Regarding those dharmas I have previously mentioned—whether wholesome or unwholesome, black or white, with fault or without fault, pertaining to the pure side or the defiled side, superior or inferior, broad or narrow—when such dharmas are to be applied according to their respective circumstances:
"O Brahmins, you are single-mindedly and stubbornly attached.
I say that such people are truly deluded, for they take their own conscious mind to be true understanding.
O laypeople!"
Furthermore, various brahmins may engage in discourse regarding caste, or discourse regarding lineage, or discourse regarding their own teachings.

They further give rise to this thought: "What others ought to do for me—such as preparing a seat, drawing water, making offerings, rising to welcome me, and joining their palms in greeting—I myself should not do for others."
I declare that a person who conceives such an intention does not see the True Dharma.
Furthermore, householder,

if there are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are attached to discourses concerning lineage and clan, or who are attached to discourses concerning their own teachings, I declare them to be śramaṇas who have not truly renounced, and brāhmaṇas who have not truly renounced.
"Householder!

There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not cling to discourse concerning lineage, nor do they cling to discourse concerning clan, nor do they cling to discourse concerning their own teachings. I declare that such individuals have truly attained liberation; they are the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess correct understanding."
"Furthermore, lay follower!
That Great King Pasenadi, the lord of Kosala, saw the Śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who had gone forth from the Śākya clan, having abandoned the household life.

"O lay follower! That King Prasenajit, toward the son of the Śākyas, felt joy and comfort; he paid homage with respectful prostrations, rose to welcome him, and, joining his palms, inquired after his well-being."

That great king Jayasena, the lord of Kośala, felt joy and comfort in the presence of the Buddha, the Tathāgata; he paid him respectful homage, rose to welcome him, and with palms joined, inquired after his well-being.
The king did not regard the śramaṇa Gautama as being of a noble lineage, nor did the king conceive the thought that he was of a noble lineage;
he did not regard the śramaṇa Gautama for his physical marks and dignified appearance, nor did the king conceive the thought of such marks and appearance;
he did not regard the śramaṇa Gautama for his great reputation, nor did the king conceive the thought of such reputation.
From this you should know that such is the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
Householder!
This Dharma is from the beginning supreme, greatest, and most preeminent.
Such right view is the fundamental matrix of all phenomena; it is supreme and the ultimate destination.
Furthermore, householder, if a person abides in right faith toward me, that person shall attain firm growth, the birth of the root, and unshakable pure faith.

Why is this? Because whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, or brahmās—indeed, all beings within the three realms—they are all my children; they all share the same Dharma, without distinction.
Born from the mouth of the True Dharma, sharing the same seed of the Dharma, and transformed by the Dharma—they are true sons of the Buddha.
O lay follower!
Someone might ask:
"Why have you all abandoned each of your respective parents, lineages, and clans?
To this, they replied:
"We are all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya."
"Householder, you should know that it is the nature of things (dharmatā) to be thus: this Dharma is from the beginning the most supreme, the greatest, and the most preeminent.
Such right view is the fundamental matrix of all phenomena; it is the sovereign, the ultimate destination."
The Sūtra on the Origins of the Two Brahmins, Śvetaketu and Suvarṇadhvaja, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One;
The Sūtra on the Origins of the Two Brahmins, Śvetaketu and Suvarṇadhvaja, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Middle.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlaguṇabhadra, Dharma-transmitting Master, Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Chamberlain for Ceremonial Affairs, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and others, under imperial decree: "Furthermore, O layman!
After an extremely long period, when this world-system was being destroyed, the sentient beings of that realm returned once more to be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
After an extremely long period, when this world-system was being formed, sentient beings from another realm passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and came to be born here.

These sentient beings each possess a bodily radiance that is pure and brilliant; they travel through the air, proceeding wherever they desire with joy and happiness, acting with sovereign mastery according to their will.
Because those sentient beings possessed radiance from their own bodies, at that time the light of the sun and moon did not appear at all in the world;
because the light of the sun and moon did not appear, the stars also did not appear;
and because the stars did not appear, the lunar mansions likewise did not appear.
Because the constellations do not appear, one does not distinguish between the differences of day and night;
because one does not distinguish the difference between day and night, there is likewise no differentiation of months, years, days, or hours.
Furthermore, there was no distinction between male and female forms.
At that time, it was the natural law for sentient beings that their bodily radiance illuminated one another.
"Moreover, O lay follower!"

At that time, great waters surged forth from the earth, their color like that of ghee or milk, and their taste like that of sugarcane or honey; they were fragrant, exquisite, and subtle, serving as food for people and nourishing their sense faculties. This was called "earth-essence" (pṛthivī-rasa).
At that time, one sentient being developed an intense fondness for this essence of the earth; taking it up with the tip of his finger, he tasted its flavor.
When the other sentient beings saw this, they did likewise, conceiving a longing desire and also tasting it with the tips of their fingers, thereby developing a similar fondness.
At that time, sentient beings developed an intense attachment to the "taste of the earth" (*pṛthivī-rasa*) and consumed it to nourish their bodies.
Because they ate much, the bodies of these sentient beings gradually became solid and coarse.
Due to this coarseness, they were no longer able to travel through the air at will, and their bodily radiance vanished.
Because the radiance of their bodies had vanished, the great earth then became entirely shrouded in darkness, and the sun and moon appeared in the world;
because the sun and moon appeared, the constellations also appeared, and day and night were first distinguished;
once day and night were distinguished, there arose the differentiations of years, months, days, and hours.
"Furthermore, lay follower!
At that time, sentient beings first ate the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*), which served as their sustenance for a long period.
Because those sentient beings who were greedy and ate excessively became emaciated and weak in physical appearance;..."
If one eats little, their physical appearance becomes full and robust.
At that time, those who are full and robust, seeing those who are emaciated and weak, do not understand the reason for it and speak thus:
"You are the one who is emaciated and weak; I am the one who is full and robust."
Because of this, they gave rise to thoughts of pride; for this reason, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) vanished.
At that time, when sentient beings saw that the essence of the earth had disappeared, they all cried out:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"Alas! Why has this taste of the earth now vanished?
"Furthermore, O lay follower!"
Once the essence of the earth had vanished, the earth-cake (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) appeared again.
Its color was like that of the *añjana* bird, its taste like sugarcane or honey, and it was fragrant, exquisite, and subtle, serving as food for human beings.
At that time, sentient beings next consumed earth-cakes as their sustenance for a long period.
Among those sentient beings, those who ate greedily became emaciated and weak in appearance,
while those who ate sparingly remained full and robust in appearance.
At that time, the one who was well-nourished, seeing the one who was emaciated and weak, did not understand the reason for it and spoke these words:
"You are the one who is emaciated and weak; I am the one who is well-nourished."
Because of this, they gave rise to thoughts of pride; for this reason, the earth-cakes vanished.
When those sentient beings saw that the earth-cakes had disappeared, they all cried out:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"Alas! Why has this cake on the ground now vanished?
"Furthermore, lay follower!"

Once the earth-cakes had vanished, forest creepers grew up again; like the branches of the *karañjaka* tree, they possessed four kinds of colors and a flavor like sugarcane or honey, fragrant, delicious, and exquisite, serving as food for human beings.
At that time, those sentient beings subsequently sustained themselves for a long period by eating forest creepers.
Among them, those who ate greedily became emaciated and weak in appearance,
while those who ate sparingly remained full and robust in appearance.
At that time, the one who was well-nourished, seeing the one who was emaciated and weak, did not know the reason for it and spoke these words:
"You are the one who is emaciated and weak; I am the one who is well-nourished."
"Because of this, they gave rise to thoughts of arrogance; for this reason, the forest creepers vanished.
At that time, when sentient beings saw that the forest creepers had disappeared, they all cried out: 'Alas!'"
"Alas! Why has this forest creeper now vanished?
"Householder! [the Buddha replied.]
In the present age, there are some people who, when encountering the suffering of the Dharma and being afflicted by it, also utter these words: "Alas!
Alas! How bitter!"
"Furthermore, lay follower!
Once the forest creepers had vanished, fragrant rice appeared.
This fragrant rice was without husks or chaff, and its exquisite fragrance was delightful."
Ripening according to the seasons, once harvested in the morning, it grows back by evening;
once harvested in the evening, it grows back by morning.
Having been taken, it immediately revives, with no interval of cessation between.
Twice daily, at dawn and dusk, they gathered fragrant rice solely for sustenance, unaware of its original cause.

At that time, sentient beings vied with one another in greedily consuming it; due to these conditions, their bodies became increasingly coarse and heavy, and the distinctions between the two sexes—male and female—emerged.
Due to this, sentient beings give rise to mutual hatred and attachment; because of this hatred and attachment, they slander one another.
Furthermore, they gradually develop mutual passionate clinging, and this clinging is the cause that serves as the root of all faults.
Furthermore, due to mutual slander, sentient beings began to strike one another with sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones.
Consequently, unrighteousness and improper conduct arose in the world.
"Householder!
Just as people of the world today take a young girl, adorn her with various flowers and deck her in exquisite garments, seeking a man of a different clan to take her as his wife."
They establish what is contrary to the Dharma as the true Dharma, yet they lack any understanding of its meaning;
the sentient beings of that time will be just like this.

What was once the true Dharma in the past will now be considered contrary to the Dharma, and what was once the Vinaya will be considered non-Vinaya; in this way, various unrighteous practices will gradually arise.

Due to engaging in unrighteous conduct, they gradually give rise to oppression, lose their sense of renunciation, and increasingly fall into indolence; for one day, two days, three days, or even up to a month, they do not remain at home nor attend to household affairs, but wander through the wilderness while concealing their transgressions and faults.
At that time, there was a man who, being by nature indolent, failed to go at the proper time to gather the fragrant rice.
He then thought to himself: "Why do I now undergo such hardship?"
"In the morning I go to gather fragrant rice, and in the evening I return to gather it again.
If I could now go but once a day to gather the fragrant rice for both the morning and evening meals, would that not be excellent?"
Having formed this thought, he immediately went and gathered the fragrant rice for both times.
Furthermore, householder!
At that time, another person came and said to him:
"Come now with me to gather the fragrant rice," [the Buddha said].
The lazy one replied, "You go alone;
I have already gathered the fragrant rice for the two meals of morning and evening."
Then, the one who had come to summon him thought to himself:
"Since it is virtuous to take the fragrant rice for two meals' worth at a time,
why do I not go now and take at once the fragrant rice for two or three days' worth?"
Having formed this thought, he went immediately to take them all together.
Furthermore, householder!
At that time, another person came and said to him:
"You should now go with me to gather fragrant rice.
The person replied, "You may go by yourself;
I have already gathered enough fragrant rice for two or three days' consumption."
At that time, the man thought to himself:
"It is already virtuous for me to go once and take enough fragrant rice for two or three days' consumption;
why do I not now go once and take enough fragrant rice for four or five days' consumption?"
Having had this thought, he went at once to gather them all together.
"Furthermore, householder!
When the fragrant rice was first harvested, it was without husks or chaff, and its fragrance was exquisite and wonderful."
Because of the cause of being indolent, he subsequently and gradually takes more and more in succession, accumulating it until it suffices for his own enjoyment.

At that time, fragrant rice gradually began to produce husks and chaff; once harvested in the morning, it did not grow again by evening, and once harvested in the evening, it did not grow again by morning. It no longer returned to life, and they did not know the cause.
Those sentient beings then gathered together and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"In the beginning, each of us possessed a bodily radiance and traveled through the air; we were happy and autonomous."

Because of the radiance of their bodies, the light of the sun, moon, and stars does not appear; furthermore, there is no distinction between day and night, nor any differentiation of years, months, days, or hours. Moreover, the physical forms of male and female are not distinguished, for it is the natural law that the radiance from the bodies of sentient beings illuminates one another.

At that time, great waters surged forth from the earth, their color like that of clarified butter or milk, and their taste like that of sugarcane or honey; they were fragrant, exquisite, and subtle. When consumed by people, they nourished and benefited the sense faculties, and were known as "earth-essence" (pṛthivī-rasa).
At that time, one sentient being, seeing it, felt intense affection and took it up with the tip of his finger to taste its flavor.
When the other sentient beings saw this, they did likewise; they all tasted its flavor and were filled with love and delight.
At that time, we used it as our food to nourish and sustain our bodies.

As we greedily consumed this essence of the earth in great quantities, our limbs gradually became coarse and heavy. For this reason, we were no longer able to travel through the air at will, and our bodily radiance vanished; consequently, the entire world fell into total darkness.
At that time, the sun, moon, and stars appeared, and their radiance emerged, for the first time distinguishing day from night.
There were also distinctions of years, months, days, and hours.
At that time, we sustained ourselves by eating the "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) for a long duration; those who ate greedily became emaciated in appearance.

If those who ate little had their physical forms become full and robust, then those who were full and robust would give rise to thoughts of pride upon seeing those who were emaciated and weak. For this reason, the flavor of the earth disappeared, and the cakes of earth appeared once more.
It was sweet, exquisite, and perfect in both color and fragrance; what we ate provided us with sustenance for a long time.
Those who ate greedily became thin and weak in appearance, while those who ate sparingly remained full and robust.

At that time, those who were well-nourished saw those who were emaciated and weak, and gave rise to thoughts of arrogance. For this reason, the earth-cakes vanished and forest creepers appeared once more.
It was sweet, delicate, and exquisite, endowed with perfect color and fragrance; what we ate has long served as our sustenance.
Those who ate greedily became thin and weak in appearance, while those who ate sparingly remained full and robust in form.

At that time, those who were well-nourished saw those who were emaciated and weak, and gave rise to thoughts of arrogance. Because of this condition, the forest creepers vanished and fragrant rice grew once more.

At that time, the fragrant rice was free of husks and chaff, its exquisite scent being most delightful; once harvested in the morning, it grew back by evening, and once harvested in the evening, it grew back by morning.

What we ate was merely for the sake of sustenance; we did not know its original cause. As our greed for food increased, the resulting waste soon became a hindrance. At that time, distinctions between male and female first appeared, followed by the arising of hatred and affection, leading to mutual slander.
Furthermore, they gradually gave rise to mutual attachment; this attachment became the root of all faults.
At that time, because we slandered one another, we struck each other with sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones.

Thereupon, in this world, unrighteousness arose; because unrighteousness arose, there gradually emerged oppression, a decline in the sense of renunciation, and a concurrent increase in indolence. For one day, two days, and even up to a month, they did not remain at home nor attend to their household affairs, but wandered through the wilderness, concealing their transgressions and faults.
At that time, there was a man who, being by nature indolent, could not go to fetch the fragrant rice at the proper times; he then thought to himself:
"Why do I now undergo such hardship, going to fetch the fragrant rice every morning and returning to fetch it again every evening?"
"I should now go once every day to gather the fragrant rice for both the morning and evening meals at one time.
Having formed this thought, he went and gathered it all at once.
At that time, another person came and said to him:
"Come now with me and let us go to gather the fragrant rice.
The lazy one replied, "You may go by yourself; I have already gathered the fragrant rice for two times."
At that time, the person thought to himself:
"It is good to gather fragrant rice twice a day; now, on my single journey, I shall gather enough for two or three days."
Having had this thought, he went immediately to gather them together.
At that time, another person came and said to him, "Come now with me;
let us go to gather the fragrant rice."
The other person replied, "You need only go yourself; I have already brought back the three-day-old fragrant rice.
At that time, the man thought to himself:
"Regarding the taking of three days' worth of fragrant rice as being sufficient, I shall now go and take enough for four or five days.
Having formed this thought, he went at once and took it all at once.

"You all should know that when they first took the fragrant rice, it was without husks or chaff. Later, as they gradually took more and began to store it away, the fragrant rice gradually developed husks and chaff.

What had been harvested in the morning would not grow back by evening, and what had been harvested in the evening would not grow back by morning; it no longer returned to life, and they did not understand the cause."
"At this time, we should collectively divide and apportion the entire earth-element into equal portions, establishing boundaries for each:
'This is your territory; this is my territory.'"
After those people had deliberated with one another, they immediately divided the boundaries and established them as limits.
The Buddha said,
“Lay follower!
At that time, after the multitude had divided the boundaries of the land, there was a certain person who went to fetch fragrant rice; having obtained it with great difficulty, he thought to himself:
"How can I now obtain food?"
"How shall I sustain my life?
My own portion of fragrant rice is now nearly exhausted; although there is some in other fields, they do not permit it to be taken. I must now go and steal a small portion from them."
Having had this thought, he carefully guarded his own fragrant rice and went to another realm to steal the fragrant rice.
When the owner saw him, he said to the thief: "Hey!..."
"You are a thief! For what reason have you come here to steal my fragrant rice?
The thief replied, "I am not such a person;
I have never taken the fragrant rice from within your domain."
"Furthermore, at a second time, when that person went to fetch the fragrant rice, it was likewise difficult to find. He then gave rise to this thought:
'How shall I now obtain food to eat?'"
"How shall I sustain my life?
My own portion of fragrant rice is now nearly exhausted; although there is some in another field, they will not permit me to take it. I must now go and steal a small portion from them."
Having formed this thought, he secured his own fragrant rice with great care and went to another realm to steal the fragrant rice.
When its owner saw him again and he had returned to steal it for a second time, the owner spoke to him once more:
"You are a thief! For what reason have you come here again to steal my fragrant rice?
The thief replied, "I am not like that;
I have never taken the fragrant rice from within your realm."
The Sūtra on the Origins of the Two Brahmins Śuklodana and Suvarṇadhvaja, Spoken by the Buddha, Middle Volume.
The Sūtra on the Origins of the Two Brahmins Śuklodana and Suvarṇadhvaja, Spoken by the Buddha,
Final Volume.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma-transmitting Master and Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Subject Śramaṇa Shi Hu, and others, by imperial decree: "Furthermore, layman!
At that third period, when the predecessors went again to fetch the fragrant rice, it was likewise difficult to obtain;
they then thought to themselves: "How can we now obtain our food?"
"How shall I sustain my life?
My own portion of fragrant rice is now nearly exhausted; although there is some in another field, they will not permit me to take it. I shall now steal a small portion from that."
Having had this thought, he protected his own fragrant rice with great care, yet began to commit thefts from the territory of others.
When the owner saw him come here three times to commit such thefts, anger arose in his heart, and he spoke these words:
"You thief! For what reason have you come here three times to commit theft!
He then seized the man's two hands and raised his staff to strike him; as the thief was beaten, he cried out and wept.
At that time in the world, non-Dharma arose and various improper conducts emerged; from this, the name "staff and cudgel" was first established.

Because of that theft, there arise such things as anger and affliction; this is what constitutes unrighteousness (*adharma*). Since unrighteousness arises, improper conduct flourishes, and from this, three unwholesome factors (*akuśala-dharma*) are first established: namely, theft, false speech, and the use of the staff (violence).
"Furthermore, lay follower!
At that time, when the multitude of people saw this occurrence, they gathered once more and deliberated among themselves, saying:
'In the beginning, our bodies possessed radiance, and we were sovereign according to our desires.'"
Because of the radiance of his body, the sun, moon, and stars all ceased to appear; day and night were no longer distinguished, nor were there any differences between years, months, days, or hours.
At that time, great waters surged forth from the earth, known as "earth-essence" (*pṛthivī-rasa*); we consumed it, and it served as our sustenance for a long time.

Finally, because we ourselves gave rise to unwholesome states, the earth-essence vanished and "earth-cake" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) appeared; we took this and ate it, and it served as our sustenance for a long time.

Finally, because we ourselves gave rise to unwholesome states, the earth-cake vanished and "forest-vines" (*vanalatā*) appeared; we took these and ate them, and they served as our sustenance for a long time.

Finally, because we ourselves gave rise to unwholesome states, the forest creepers vanished and fragrant rice appeared again—free from husks and without chaff—which we took as food for our long-term sustenance.

Finally, because we ourselves gave rise to unwholesome states, husks and chaff grew upon that fragrant rice; what was harvested in the morning did not grow back by evening, and what was harvested in the evening did not grow back by morning. It no longer regrew, and we did not know the cause.
At that time, we divided the territory equally with fragrant rice.

Once the boundaries had been demarcated, there was a man who went to gather fragrant rice and obtained it with great difficulty; he then committed theft within another's domain. When the owner saw this, he said to the thief: "Hey!..."
"You are a thief! For what reason have you come here to commit theft?
The thief replied, "It is not so;
I have never stolen the fragrant rice from your realm."
Furthermore, when the first person stole the fragrant rice a second and a third time, it was likewise.
Upon seeing this, the owner became enraged and spoke these words:
"Hey! You!"
"You thief! For what reason have you come here three times to steal?
He then seized the man's two hands, raised his staff, and struck him. As the thief was being beaten, he cried out and wept.
At that time in the world, unrighteousness arose, and various improper conducts came into being; from this, the name "staff" (daṇḍa) emerged.
The three unwholesome dharmas were first established: namely, theft, false speech, and the use of the staff (violence).
"At this time, it would be fitting for us all to select one who is endowed with perfect physical marks, great majesty, and great wisdom, and establish him as the Lord of the Fields.
We, all of us, shall each take one portion of our own field's fragrant rice and give it to him."

This person is impartial and upright; those who should be disciplined, he disciplines, and those who should be gathered under his care, he gathers. He protects the land and protects the people; we should each receive his instructions accordingly.

At that time, once the assembly had reached a consensus through deliberation, they collectively selected one who was endowed with perfect physical characteristics, great majesty, and great wisdom, and established him as the Lord of the Fields to act as their sovereign; all the people then accepted his authority.
The Buddha said,
"Layman! At that time,
because he was established by the consent of the multitude, he was therefore called the 'Field Lord Approved by the Multitude'."
The name "Lord of the Fields" was the first to fall among the enumeration of written words.
Furthermore, because he performed excellent protection over the realm of earth and acted as its sovereign, he was called a *kṣatriya*;
this name "kṣatriya" was the second to fall among the enumeration of written words.
Furthermore, because one can produce words of reconciliation and consolation from among all virtues, one is called a "consoler"; this consoler is precisely what is meant by a "king.
This name "king" is the third to fall within the enumeration of written characters.
At this time, in this world, the realm of the kṣatriyas was first established.

Householder, you should know that whether these or those sentient beings are alike or different, whether they act according to the Dharma or contrary to the Dharma, despite their differences, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that is most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime; seeing such a Dharma, such a Dharma arises, and they take it as their superior refuge and goal.
"Furthermore, lay follower!

At that time, there was later one person among the assembly who, seeing that unreal phenomena were oppressive and diminishing, immediately gave rise to weary detachment and abandoned the ways of household life."
Thereupon, in a secluded place within the wilderness, he constructed a grass hut and, fixing his mind on a single point, practiced meditative concentration and tranquility.
At the time of sunset, for the sake of food and drink, he entered the village;
and again at dawn, for the sake of food and drink, he returned to the village.
When the other people saw this person, they thought to themselves:

"This person, having perceived that dharmas are unreal, has been oppressed by them and diminished; yet he has immediately conceived a sense of weary detachment and abandoned the ways of household life."
"Thereupon, in a secluded place in the wilderness, he constructed a grass hut, fixed his mind on a single point, and practiced meditative tranquility (śamatha).

Thus he was first called a 'practitioner of meditation. Later, he was further named a 'boisterous person. Later, he was further named a 'meditator who is boisterous. Later, he was further named a 'giver of instructions. And later, he was further named a 'doer of unwholesome deeds.'"
"Furthermore, lay follower!

At that time, among the assembly, there was another class of people who, having initially practiced meditation, later returned to conceptualizing through mental attention; they settled within villages, established boundaries, gathered disciples, and taught the classical texts."
When the other people saw this man, they said to one another:

"This person first practiced meditative stillness in the wilderness, but later returned to active mental engagement; he now dwells within a village, establishing boundaries and gathering disciples to instruct them in the classical texts."
This is not what is called a practitioner of dhyāna; at that time, he was designated as a "teacher" (śāstr) and also called a "Brahmin who speaks much.
This name "Brahmin" was the first to fall into the category of written characters.
For this reason, there exists in the world a certain sphere for the class of *brāhmaṇas*.
Householder!

You should know that whether they be such or other, whether they be various sentient beings, whether they be alike or different, whether they be in accordance with the Dharma or contrary to it—despite these distinctions, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), it is spontaneously so: most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime. Seeing such a Dharma, such a Dharma arises; one takes refuge in it as the preeminent goal.
"Furthermore, lay follower!

At that time, there was another class of people among the multitude who extensively sowed seeds in the fields and engaged in agricultural labor to sustain their lives; because they performed the work of sowing in the fields, they were called Vaiśyas.
This name 'Vaiśya' was the first to fall into the category of written characters."
For this reason, there exists in the world a certain class of realm known as the Vaiśyas.

Householder, you should know that whether they be such or others, among all classes of sentient beings—whether similar or different, whether in accordance with the Dharma or contrary to it—despite their distinctions, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is spontaneously so: most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime. Seeing such a Dharma, such a Dharma arises, leading them toward a superior destination.
"Furthermore, lay follower!
At that time, within that assembly, another class of people gradually arose who were skillful in deceit and engaged in various evil deeds; they were called Śūdras.
This name 'Śūdra' was for the first time included among the categories of written characters, and from this, there came to be the realm of the Śūdra class in the world."
"O lay follower!

You should know that whether they be this or that, whether sentient beings be similar or different, and whether their actions be in accordance with the Dharma or contrary to it—despite these distinctions—the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is spontaneous, most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime. Seeing such phenomena, such phenomena arise; thus one attains the ultimate refuge."
"Furthermore, lay follower!

Among those of the kṣatriya caste, there are those who renounce the world, out of weariness with and aversion for oppression, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, hardship, danger, and calamity; they abandon their homes to go forth as monastics—these are my śramaṇas.
It was among the kṣatriya caste that this name 'śramaṇa' was first applied."

Having practiced in this manner, those who were Brahmins, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras likewise did so; if, out of weariness with oppression, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, hardship, and calamity, they abandoned their homes to go forth and all became śramaṇas without distinction, it was thereby that the first establishment of the single class of śramaṇas in the world came to be.
"O lay follower!

You should know that whether they be this or that, all classes of sentient beings—whether similar or different, whether in accordance with the Dharma or contrary to it—though there be distinctions, by the very nature of things (dharmatā), spontaneously, most supremely, most excellently, and most loftily, upon seeing such a Dharma, such a Dharma arises, and they attain a superior refuge."
The Buddha said, "Householder!

Following this sequence, there are five categories of realms that were first established in this world; namely, the realm of the kṣatriyas, the realm of the brāhmaṇas, the realm of the vaiśyas, the realm of the śūdras, and the realm of the śramaṇas."
Among these five, the śramaṇa is the most honored and supreme, possessing a vast reputation that none can surpass.
Householder!

It is like a high peak, exceedingly lofty and steep; even if there were a herd of oxen wandering all around that peak, capable of going everywhere, yet if they wished to rush to its summit, they would ultimately be unable to reach it.
And that mountain peak is, by its very nature, the most supreme, the greatest, and the most preeminent and lofty.

Those five objects of experience are likewise so; yet the domain of the śramaṇa is, by its very nature, the most supreme, the greatest, and the most preeminent and lofty among all worlds, with nothing superior to it.
"Furthermore, lay follower!

Among those of the kṣatriya caste, there are those who, having committed unwholesome deeds of body as well as unwholesome deeds of speech and mind, give rise to wrong views; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil destinies and are reborn in hell."

The same applies to the various castes of Brahmins, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras: if they commit unwholesome deeds of body, as well as unwholesome deeds of speech and mind, and give rise to wrong views, then at the breaking up of the body after death, they will fall into the evil destinies and be reborn in hell.

It is the same for a śramaṇa: having committed unwholesome deeds of body, as well as unwholesome deeds of speech and mind, and having given rise to wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, he falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell.
Furthermore, householder!

Among those of the kṣatriya caste, there are those who, having performed various bodily actions and various verbal and mental actions, give rise to various views; when their bodies dissolve and their lives end, they are reborn among human beings.

Furthermore, among the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those who are śramaṇas, it is likewise for all such classes: having performed various types of bodily karma as well as various types of verbal and mental karma, and having given rise to various views, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among human beings.
"Furthermore, lay follower!

Among those of the kṣatriya caste, there are those who, having performed wholesome deeds of body as well as wholesome deeds of speech and mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in the heavenly realms."

Furthermore, among the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those who are śramaṇas, it is likewise for all such classes: having performed wholesome deeds of body, as well as wholesome deeds of speech and mind, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavenly realms.
"Furthermore, lay follower!

Having cultivated wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, that kṣatriya gives rise to right view; dwelling with a settled mind upon the four foundations of mindfulness and having practiced the seven factors of enlightenment according to principle, he is able to personally realize that realm of nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, whether they be Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those who are śramaṇas—all such classes likewise do so. Having cultivated wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, they give rise to right view; dwelling with a settled mind upon the four foundations of mindfulness and having practiced the seven factors of enlightenment according to principle, they are able to personally realize that realm of nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, lay follower!
At that first time, the Great Brahmā King spoke this verse:
'Among the kṣatriya clan he is the most honored; His lineage is true and moreover pure.'"
"Having perfected all three types of supernormal knowledge, he is the most excellent Honored One among humans and devas. "Householder!
The gāthā spoken by that Great Brahmā King is well-spoken and well-sung; these words are truthful and not falsely uttered."
Why is this? For I also proclaim:

"The Kṣatriya caste is the most honored among humans; their lineage is authentic and furthermore pure; they are fully perfected in the three types of knowledge and all practices; among gods and humans, they are the most venerable and supreme."
At that time, the two brahmins, Śuklodana and Kāñcanavatsa, joined their palms in reverence and approached the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In the past, we were shrouded by ignorance and could not awaken to ourselves."
We were like those who are hunched over, like those who are deluded, and like those in deep darkness; we were unable to penetrate anything we turned toward.

Today, having received the World-Honored Buddha’s instruction on the correct principle and his analytical exposition, we have suddenly awakened—like those who are hunched gaining full extension, the deluded receiving guidance, and those in darkness finding a torch.

From this day forward, I vow to take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the True Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. As a lay follower of the World-Honored One, until the end of my life, I shall uphold the Buddha’s Dharma as I would protect my own life; I shall always possess a sense of shame and remorse, and with compassion for sentient beings—even down to ants—I shall give rise to thoughts of protective mindfulness.
"I have now followed the Buddha to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!"
"Now these two brahmins, Śvetaketu and Suvarṇadhvaja, have gone forth from the household life to join the Buddha.
You bhikṣus, you should confer the full ordination upon them."
Then, at the Buddha’s command, the bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon them.
In that very instant, the two brahmins, the White-Robed One and the Golden-Bannered One, assumed the appearance of bhikṣus and became fully endowed with virtuous conduct.

At that time, the two bhikṣus, the Venerable Pāṇḍuka and Cūḍapanthaka, focused their minds on a single object, free from all distraction; purifying their bodies and minds and seeking the true principle, they immediately attained the three types of supernormal knowledge: the divine eye, the recollection of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows.
Having attained the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*), this one of right understanding hears the Dharma that has been taught and gains great benefit.
*The Sūtra on the Origins of the Two Brahmins, Śuklodana and Suvarṇadhvaja*, translated by the Buddha, Volume Lower.
